chapters.name: Chapter 1: How EVs work and how to stay safe

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The parts of an electric vehicle
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main parts of an EV and say what each one does.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list or drawing of EV parts, you will name the main parts of an electric vehicle and say what each one does, getting at least 5 of 6 parts right.
An electric vehicle (EV) runs on electricity stored in a large high-voltage battery pack, usually under the floor. On many EVs this battery works at about 400 to 1,000 volts. That is far more than a home outlet, and it can kill.
The battery stores DC power. An inverter changes it into the AC the electric motor uses. The motor turns the wheels. When the driver slows down, the motor works backward as a generator and puts some energy back in the battery. This is regenerative braking.
The onboard charger changes AC from a charging station into DC to fill the battery. A DC-to-DC converter steps the high voltage down to charge the normal 12-volt battery, which still runs the lights, radio and computers. High-voltage cables are usually bright orange.
A hybrid (HEV) has both a gas engine and an electric motor with a smaller battery. A plug-in hybrid (PHEV) has a bigger battery you can charge from a plug, plus a gas engine.
Words to know:
- EV (electric vehicle): a vehicle that runs only on electricity from a battery.
- Hybrid (HEV): a vehicle with a gas engine and an electric motor that does not plug in.
- Plug-in hybrid (PHEV): a hybrid with a bigger battery you can charge from a plug.
- High-voltage battery pack: the big battery that powers the motor; it can be deadly.
- Inverter: the part that changes DC from the battery into AC for the motor.
- Regenerative braking: slowing the car by using the motor as a generator, which puts energy back in the battery.
- Onboard charger: the part in the car that changes AC from a charger into DC for the battery.
- DC-to-DC converter: the part that steps high voltage down to charge the 12-volt battery.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center: Maintenance and safety of electric vehicles
Try it now: On paper, draw a simple car from the side. Draw and label six parts: high-voltage battery pack, inverter, electric motor, onboard charger, DC-to-DC converter and 12-volt battery. Draw the orange cables in a different color. Next to each part, write one line about what it does.
You can now name the main parts of an EV and say what each one does.

check.q: What color are high-voltage cables on EVs usually?
check.why: High-voltage cables are typically bright orange so workers can spot the danger.

options: Uses the motor to slow the car and put energy back in the battery
Charges the car from a gas tank
check.why: The motor acts as a generator when slowing, sending energy back to the battery.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: High-voltage safety: know when to stop
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the high-voltage hazards in a shop and the safety rule for each one.
This lesson builds toward: Given a shop scenario with an EV, you will list the high-voltage hazards and the safety rule for each one, including "do not touch orange cables or the battery pack without training" and lockout/tagout.
The high-voltage system can cause electric shock, burns and arc flash. It can stay dangerous after the car is turned off, and a damaged battery can catch fire, even hours or days later.
The first rule for a new worker: do not touch orange cables, the battery pack, or any part with a high-voltage warning label. Only trained, authorized technicians work on the high-voltage system. They follow the manufacturer's service information to shut the system down, wait the time it gives, and test that it is dead.
Trained technicians wear insulated gloves rated for the voltage, checked before every use, and use lockout/tagout so no one can turn the power back on while they work. OSHA's lockout/tagout rule is 29 CFR 1910.147.
Other shop rules still apply: lift the car only at the manufacturer's lift points (the battery pack is underneath), keep the area clear, and tell a supervisor about any damaged, leaking, smoking or hot battery. Get away from it and do not try to fix it.
Step by step:
- Look for orange cables and high-voltage warning labels.
- Do not touch them unless you are trained and authorized.
- Lift only at the manufacturer's lift points.
- Report any damaged, hot, smoking or leaking battery and move away.
- Trained techs: shut down, wait, test, lock out and tag out, per the service information.
Words to know:
- Electric shock: injury when electricity passes through your body.
- Arc flash: a sudden blast of heat and light from electricity jumping through the air.
- Authorized: allowed by your employer because you have the right training.
- Insulated gloves: special rubber gloves rated to protect against a certain voltage.
- Lockout/tagout: steps that shut off and lock power so no one can turn it back on while work is done.
- Service information: the manufacturer's official repair steps for a vehicle.
- Lift point: the spot under a car where it is safe to lift it.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)
- U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center: EV safety and emergency response
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
Try it now: Practice scenario: an EV comes in after a fender bender. There is a dent under the car near the battery and a sharp smell. A coworker says, "Just unplug that orange cable so we can lift it." On paper, make a two-column list: Hazard and What I do. Write at least four rows.
You can now spot high-voltage hazards in a shop and say the safety rule for each one, including when to stop and get a trained technician.

check.q: You are new and see an orange cable under a car you are working on. What do you do?
options: Pull it out of the way
Do not touch it; tell a trained technician
check.why: Orange cables carry high voltage; only trained, authorized technicians work on them.

options: Making sure no one can turn the power back on during work
check.why: Lockout/tagout keeps power off while someone works on the system.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Charging basics and charging math (practice only)
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the energy needed and the charging time from practice numbers.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice battery and charger numbers, you will calculate the energy needed and the charging time, with no math errors, showing your work.
There are three common charging levels in the US. Level 1 uses a normal 120-volt outlet and is slow. Level 2 uses 240 volts at homes or 208 volts at many businesses; it is the most common public charger. DC fast charging sends DC straight to the battery and is the fastest.
Common plugs are J1772 (Level 1 and 2), CCS (J1772 plus two pins for DC fast charging) and J3400, also called NACS, based on Tesla's design. Installing a charger at a home or business is electrical work for a licensed electrician.
Battery size is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). Charger power is in kilowatts (kW). Practice formula: hours = kWh needed / charger kW. All numbers here are made up for practice only. Real charging slows down as the battery gets full, and losses make it take longer.
Step by step:
- Find the battery size in kWh.
- Work out how much of it you need: battery kWh x (percent to add / 100).
- Divide the kWh needed by the charger's kW.
- Write the answer in hours and say it is an estimate.
Words to know:
- Level 1: slow charging from a normal 120-volt outlet.
- Level 2: faster charging at 240 or 208 volts.
- DC fast charging: the fastest charging, sending DC straight to the battery.
- Kilowatt-hour (kWh): a measure of energy; battery size is in kWh.
- Kilowatt (kW): a measure of power; charger speed is in kW.
- J1772, CCS, J3400 (NACS): names of common EV charging plugs in the US.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center: Charging electric vehicles
- EVITP: Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program (for licensed electricians)
Try it now: Practice only. Solve on paper and show your work: (a) An 80 kWh battery goes from 20% to 80%. How many kWh is that? (b) How long would that take on a 9.6 kW Level 2 charger? (c) A 40 kWh battery needs 10 kWh on a 1.25 kW Level 1 outlet. How many hours? Answers to check yourself: (a) 48 kWh, (b) 5 hours, (c) 8 hours.
You can now name the charging levels and plugs, and estimate charging time from practice numbers.

check.q: Practice only: you need 24 kWh and the charger gives 6 kW. About how long?
Which charging level uses a normal 120-volt household outlet?

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Service work and your path to the job

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Everyday EV service tasks
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a low-voltage service checklist for an EV that follows the manufacturer's service information.
This lesson builds toward: Given an EV in for routine service, you will write a low-voltage service checklist that follows the manufacturer's service information, with at least 6 correct items and no high-voltage tasks.
EVs need less upkeep than gas cars: no oil changes, spark plugs or exhaust. But they still need service, and much of it is low-voltage work a new technician can learn.
Tires: EVs are often heavy, so check tire pressure, tread and wear, and rotate tires as the maker says. Brakes: regenerative braking means pads wear slowly, but brakes still need to be checked, and parts that are used little can rust or stick. Also check wipers, lights, suspension and steering parts, the cabin air filter and the 12-volt battery.
Some EVs use liquid coolant for the battery and electronics. Checks and changes follow the manufacturer's schedule and steps; never open a high-voltage cooling part unless you are trained.
Always use the manufacturer's service information for the exact car: the schedule, the lift points and the steps. If a task touches anything orange or labeled high voltage, stop and hand it to a trained technician.
Step by step:
- Look up the service information for the exact make, model and year.
- Lift only at the listed lift points.
- Check tires, brakes, wipers, lights, suspension and steering.
- Check the cabin air filter and the 12-volt battery.
- Check coolant only as the service information says.
- Stop and hand off anything orange or labeled high voltage.
Words to know:
- Low-voltage: the normal 12-volt systems, like lights and the radio, which are safer to work on.
- Tire rotation: moving tires to different spots so they wear evenly.
- Cabin air filter: the filter that cleans air coming into the car's cabin.
- Coolant: the liquid that keeps parts from getting too hot.
- Service schedule: the maker's list of what to check and when.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center: Maintenance of electric vehicles
Try it now: Pick any EV model you have seen. On paper, write a service checklist with at least 8 items for a routine visit. Mark each one LV (low-voltage, OK for you) or STOP (high-voltage, hand off). Then check: did you put anything orange in the LV column? Fix it if you did.
You can now write a low-voltage EV service checklist and say which jobs to hand to a trained high-voltage technician.

check.q: Which job does an EV NOT need?
check.why: A battery-electric vehicle has no engine oil to change.

check.q: Where do you find the right lift points and service schedule for an EV?
options: The manufacturer's service information for that exact car
check.why: The manufacturer's service information has the correct lift points and schedule.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Certifications and training for EV work
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the certification steps toward EV technician work, with the official source for each.
This lesson builds toward: Using ase.com and other official pages, you will list the certification steps toward EV technician work, naming the source page for each step.
Most auto technicians start with a training program at a high school, community college or technical school, or begin as a lube or tire tech and learn on the job. Apprenticeships and manufacturer training programs are other ways in.
ASE (the National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence) offers the best-known technician certifications. Its L3 test, Light Duty Hybrid/Electric Vehicle Specialist, covers diagnosing the battery system, the drive system, power electronics and more. Before you can register for L3, you must pass A6 (Electrical/Electronic Systems) and A8 (Engine Performance). ASE certification also needs hands-on work experience; check the current rules on ase.com.
Many carmakers also train technicians on their own EVs. Electricians who install chargers can take EVITP training, which is for licensed electricians. Fees, test rules and experience requirements change, so check each official page before you pay.
This course prepares you to start. It does not certify you.
Step by step:
- Look up local auto technology programs and apprenticeships.
- Read the ASE L3 page and note its prerequisites (A6 and A8).
- Read ASE's work experience rules.
- Ask local shops and dealers which certifications and maker trainings they want.
- Write each step, a target date and the official page.
Words to know:
- ASE: the National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence, which certifies auto technicians.
- Certification: proof that you passed a test and met the experience rules.
- Prerequisite: something you must finish before you can start the next step.
- Diagnose: find out what is wrong and why.
- EVITP: the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program, which trains licensed electricians to install chargers.
Official sources:
- ASE: L3 Light Duty Hybrid/Electric Vehicle Specialist test
- ASE: Tests
- EVITP: Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: How to become an automotive service technician
Try it now: Open the ASE L3 test page. Write down the two tests you must pass first and three topics L3 covers. Then search for an auto technology program or apprenticeship near you and write its name and web address.
You can now name the ASE path to EV work (A6, A8, then L3), say what else it needs, and find training near you on official pages.

check.q: Which ASE test is the hybrid/electric vehicle specialist test?
check.why: L3 is ASE's Light Duty Hybrid/Electric Vehicle Specialist test.

check.q: What must you pass before you register for ASE L3?
check.why: ASE requires A6 Electrical/Electronic Systems and A8 Engine Performance before L3.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your EV Tech Start Plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write an EV Tech Start Plan with dates and a résumé skills section.
This lesson builds toward: Using your notes from this course, you will write an EV Tech Start Plan with dates and a résumé skills section, meeting every row of the rubric.
Now put it all together into one page you can take to a training program, a shop or a dealer. A plan with real dates shows you are serious.
Your plan has six parts: how an EV works in your own words; your high-voltage safety rules; two practice charging problems with your work shown; a low-voltage service checklist; your certification path with dates and sources; and an "EV skills" résumé section.
For the résumé, write true things you can do now, in short bullets that start with an action word. For example: "Know the main parts of an EV and hybrid drive system." "Trained in high-voltage safety awareness: identify orange cables and stop for a qualified tech." "Can estimate charging time from battery and charger size." Add past work that helps: car care, tire or lube work, military vehicles, electrical helper work or warehouse equipment.
Veterans: many military vehicle and electrical skills transfer. Ask a local workforce center about training help.
Step by step:
- Write your 3 to 4 sentence explanation of how an EV works.
- Write your high-voltage safety rules.
- Add two practice charging problems with your work.
- Add your low-voltage service checklist.
- Write your certification path with target dates and source pages.
- Write 3 résumé bullets that start with an action word.
Words to know:
- Résumé: a short document that lists your skills, work and training for employers.
- Target date: the day you plan to finish a step.
- Workforce center: a free public office that helps people find jobs and training; many are called American Job Centers.
Official sources:
- CareerOneStop: Find an American Job Center
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page EV Tech Start Plan with all six parts. Put a real date next to every training and certification step, and the web address for each requirement you checked. Read your résumé bullets out loud as if you were in an interview.
You can now show a shop or training program a written plan for starting EV work, with dates, sources and a résumé skills section.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds How an EV works Misses the battery pack or the inverter, or mixes up their jobs. Names the battery pack, inverter, motor, onboard charger, DC-to-DC converter and 12-volt battery, and says what each does. Also explains regenerative braking and the difference between an EV, HEV and PHEV. High-voltage safety rules Does not say to stay away from orange cables and the battery pack. Says not to touch orange or labeled high-voltage parts without training, to use the manufacturer's lift points, and to report damaged batteries. Also explains shutdown, wait, test and lockout/tagout, and who is allowed to do them. Charging math A math error, or no work shown. Both problems are right, with the formula and units shown. Also says why the real time will be longer. Service checklist Includes oil changes or a high-voltage task marked as OK. At least 6 correct low-voltage items, with high-voltage tasks marked STOP. Notes that each item follows the manufacturer's service information for the exact car. Certification path No dates, or steps with no source. Names a training route and ASE A6, A8 and L3, each with a target date and web address. Adds a maker training program or local employer and a backup plan. Résumé section Bullets are vague or claim a certification the learner does not have. Three true bullets that start with an action word and match EV shop work. Connects past work (car care, military vehicles, electrical) to EV tasks. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is the best résumé bullet for an entry-level EV shop job?
options: "Can estimate charging time from battery and charger size."
check.why: It is true and specific; never claim a certification you do not have.

check.q: Your plan says "Get ASE certified." What makes it stronger?
options: Naming A6, A8 and L3 with target dates and the ase.com page
check.why: Named tests, dates and the official source turn a wish into a plan.
